scriptwriter.title_working: Why Does Britain Drive on the Left?

chapters.title: The Puzzle
chapters.text: Take a taxi in London, and the driver sits on the right. Every single car on the road keeps to the left. Now cross the Channel to Paris, and everything flips. Same cars, same roads, same century. Opposite rules. And London is not alone. Around seventy-five countries drive on the left, and roughly one in three people on Earth live in them. So if most of the world drives on the right, why do so many still keep left? The answer is not really about safety. It is about money… and about who your neighbors are. In this video: swords on old roads, giant American wagons, the morning Sweden switched sides, and the island that switched the other way.

chapters.title: Swords and Laws
chapters.text: Let's start with the most popular theory. For centuries, travelers kept to the left. Most people are right-handed, so keeping left left your sword hand facing whoever came the other way. Historians argue about how true that story really is. But we do know exactly when Britain wrote the habit down. In seventeen seventy-three, the General Highways Act encouraged keeping left. Then the Highway Act of eighteen thirty-five made it the law. And as the British Empire spread, the rule travelled with it. To India, to Australia, to New Zealand, and to much of Africa.

chapters.title: Wagons and Napoleon
chapters.text: So why did America end up on the right? Here, the story turns on a very large wagon. In the late seventeen hundreds, freight moved in huge Conestoga wagons, pulled by teams of horses. The driver often had no seat. He rode the rear horse on the left, so his right hand was free for the whip. Sitting on the left, he wanted oncoming wagons to pass on his left, where he could watch the wheels. So the wagons kept right. Britain had fewer giant wagons, and more small carriages and riders. In Europe, a popular story gives the credit to Napoleon. Where his armies went, people kept right. Historians still debate how much of that is legend. Either way, by the twentieth century the world had split into two camps. And once a country picks a side, something powerful happens.

chapters.title: The Price of Switching
chapters.text: Every car is built for one side. Every road sign, bus door, motorway exit and traffic light faces one direction. So switching is not just a new rule on paper. It means changing millions of things at once. Economists call this a switching cost. And the more your neighbors drive on one side, the more it pays to match them. Trade, tourists and imported cars all flow more easily. That is called a network effect.

chapters.title: Sweden and Samoa
chapters.text: Sweden drove on the left, while its land neighbors, Norway and Finland, drove on the right. In nineteen fifty-five, Swedes voted on switching. About eighty-three percent said no. The government switched anyway. On the third of September, nineteen sixty-seven, at five in the morning, the whole country moved to the right. About three hundred and fifty thousand signs had to change. Now the twist. In two thousand nine, the Pacific island of Samoa did the exact opposite. It switched from the right… to the left. Why? Its big neighbors, Australia and New Zealand, drive on the left. Their used cars are built for the left, and they were far cheaper to bring in. But about three in four cars on the island were still built for the right. There were protests, and even a court case. The switch went ahead anyway, in September two thousand nine.

chapters.title: The Lesson
chapters.text: So the side of the road was never really about swords or safety. It is about what everyone around you already does, and what it would cost to change. Sweden paid a fortune to match its neighbors. Samoa switched to get cheaper cars. And Britain stays left, because changing would cost more than staying.
